  • In a recent development, AI companies and their executives seek to assuage the misgivings with a growing trove of essays, white papers, open letters, and proposals averring good intentions and pledging diligent self-control.
  • The transformational potential of artificial intelligence has bred fevered debates over safety, ethics, and accountability, fed by fears about the impact of powerful, inscrutable, and potentially uncontrollable technologies on democracy, personal agency, psychological well-being, and even human survival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

The transformational potential of artificial intelligence has bred fevered debates over safety, ethics, and accountability, fed by fears about the impact of powerful, inscrutable, and potentially uncontrollable technologies on democracy, personal agency, psychological well-being, and even human survival.

In a recent development, AI companies and their executives seek to assuage the misgivings with a growing trove of essays, white papers, open letters, and proposals averring good intentions and pledging diligent self-control. Anthropic’s form S-1, filed in October, details its public-benefit commitments and vows regarding ethics and safety. OpenAI updated its “Model Spec” late last month based on the “core values” of serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom, and “taking their circumstances seriously.”.

The transformational potential of artificial intelligence has bred fevered debates over safety, ethics, and accountability, fed by fears about the impact of powerful, inscrutable, and potentially uncontrollable technologies on democracy, personal agency, psychological well-being, and even human survival.

Industry observers note that AI companies and their executives seek to assuage the misgivings with a growing trove of essays, white papers, open letters, and proposals averring good intentions and pledging diligent self-control. Anthropic’s form S-1, filed in October, details its public-benefit commitments and vows regarding ethics and safety. OpenAI updated its “Model Spec” late last month based on the “core values” of serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom, and “taking their circumstances seriously.”.

Sources indicate that nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—the now-embattled target of a suspected Chinese spying operation—has been a champion of this laissez-faire approach, arguing that “the companies that are developing these technologies are perfectly incentivized to do the right thing,” making further regulation superfluous. In late September, the White House chimed in, imposing no newly introduced constraints and trumpeting what President Donald Trump stated would be “a tremendous self-policing aspect.”.

Yet this blizzard of pledges and manifestos seems to be doing little to reassure the public (or even key AI personnel, some of whom have resigned in alarm) that society can contain the technology’s risks. A September Quinnipiac University poll found that 74 percent of respondents held little or no trust in the leaders of AI companies. An Anthropic study published in June found that just 15 percent of Americans trust AI companies to make decisions about how the technology is developed and used.

Regulators, confronting a protean, fast-evolving technology, are facing the limits of their own competence, afraid that the wrong constraints could hamper global competitiveness and economic prosperity.

As it turns out, we are in luck, or at least potentially so. Fifteen years ago, governments unanimously endorsed a framework for addressing the human rights responsibilities of global companies. The technology industry has largely failed to incorporate these precepts into AI governance. While no panacea, it could guide a more robust, principled, and accountable approach to AI.

Sources indicate that U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan (left) and John Ruggie, special advisor to the secretary-general, arrive to attend a meeting of the Global Compact Summit at U.N. headquarters in New York on June 24, 2004.Eskinder Debebe/United Nations.

The modern human rights movement emerged from a ravaged world in which governments subordinated individual lives to national ambitions, ideological supremacy, and other grand designs. The U.N. Charter, signed in June 1945, affirmed the “dignity and worth of the human person.” Human beings possessed inviolable rights, irrespective of their standing, power, or capabilities.

That principle acquires new relevance as machines begin to rival and surpass human capacities. Superior intelligence confers no inherent authority to govern human lives, and companies must not take steps that effectively cede such dominions. The human rights tradition offers a foundation for insisting that people retain the ability to make consequential choices, exercise independent judgment, and determine which powers may be entrusted to machines.

According to recent reports, the articulation of human rights initially focused on constraining governments. As multinational corporations expanded their reach, protecting individuals also required holding private enterprises accountable. Global supply chains, extractive industries, and low-wage operations in places with weak legal protections exposed serious gaps in corporate responsibility.

In 2005, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed Harvard University professor and former U.N. official John Ruggie to set out the human rights responsibilities of multinational businesses. The resulting U.N. Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, unanimously endorsed by the Human Rights Council in 2011 and applicable across all industries, translated the foundational commitment to human dignity into practical expectations for how companies should operate.

Annan and Ruggie’s premise—that corporate needs and imperatives must be subordinate to the rights of humans—is one that demands reinforcement in an AI age where corporate creations show signs of challenging human dominance.

In a recent development, ruggie’s paradigm centered on three pillars: “Protect” meant that states had a duty to shield people from abuses by businesses. A “respect” dimension identified a separate duty of companies to follow internationally recognized human rights standards, and the “remedy” element meant that people harmed by corporate activities should have redress.

Ruggie also introduced the idea of “human rights due diligence” to identify risks, prevent and mitigate harms, monitor results, and report on them. A key innovation was grounding corporate conduct in internationally recognized human rights rather than allowing individual companies to decide for themselves what ethical behavior should entail. Unlike the proclamations that we’ve seen from AI industry leaders, Ruggie’s U.N. guiding principles (UNGPs) focus on the rights of people who may be harmed by AI, rather than on the intentions or acts of companies or chatbots.

The UNGPs do not themselves create binding international law obligations for companies, although jurisdictions can enact laws to enshrine them, and some have. France, Germany, and Norway have passed laws requiring companies to identify and address human rights risks, and the European Union adopted a broad corporate due diligence directive in 2024.

Fixating on low-likelihood, high-impact scenarios misses the forest for the trees.

Just as British people did with steam power, the American public can shape how this technology spreads.

Beijing has a strategy. Washington has a voluntary pledge and a “Super Intelligence Force.”.

According to recent reports, the UNGPs spell out globally recognized rights—including privacy, freedom of expression, equality, and labor rights—and call on companies to assess how their operations and products affect them, including through actions of customers and business partners. For an AI developer, this would entail examining whether training data is obtained legitimately and how governments or businesses might use technologies for surveillance, repression, or discrimination.

The principles specify how companies should act on these assessments: embedding findings into product design, budgets, and commercial relationships as well as tracking whether safeguards work. Companies are to exert leverage over customers and partners to prevent abuses, restricting access to technology or terminating relationships when such efforts fail. They also provide a basis for insisting that decisions affecting fundamental rights remain subject to meaningful human control, with people able to understand, challenge, and reverse consequential automated actions.

In a recent development, several leading legacy technology companies have made commitments explicitly invoking the UNGPs. Microsoft invoked the principles in its 2013 human rights statement, and it has issued human rights reports examining generative AI and law enforcement uses; in 2025, the company disabled specified cloud and AI services used by a unit of Israel’s Defense Ministry following revelations that its systems were being used in mass surveillance of Palestinians.

After scandals involving the platform’s complicity in acts of genocide in Myanmar and mass privacy breaches, Meta adopted an ambitious 2021 corporate human rights policy grounded in the guiding principles. Meta established an Oversight Board (of which I am a member) to scrutinize its adherence to human rights standards in content moderation. But its mandate limits probing investigation into broad challenges such as privacy or effects on youth. Thus far, the Oversight Board’s jurisdiction has not been extended to AI-native products such as Muse.

In a recent development, protesters hold placards warning of the human rights dangers of artificial intelligence during a rally in Amsterdam on March 8. Ana Fernandez/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images.

Meanwhile, some frontier AI labs do evince awareness of human rights obligations, but they generally treat these duties as aspirational rather than obligatory. Anthropic drew on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in drafting Claude’s constitution, while a recent DeepMind Institute essay mused that responsibilities to secure AI access might “fan outwards” from governments to technology companies.

The U.N. human rights office has proposed that AI developers vet high-risk customers before granting access to their models, write human rights safeguards into licenses, and enlist independent researchers and affected communities to evaluate whether safety measures actually work. Two reports to the Human Rights Council in 2025 proposed compelled disclosure of model capabilities, limitations and data provenance, and bans on mass surveillance and social scoring.

Most strikingly, one report recommends shifting the burden of proof for alleged AI-related harms from victims to companies, since the systems’ opacity will make it virtually impossible for owners to prove ill intent or even negligence.

In a recent development, the UNGPs elaborate several further steps to make human rights adherence rigorous: They call for companies to draw on evidence from independent stakeholders to assess whether they are meeting their human rights obligations, and to make disclosures sufficient to allow outsiders to render their own judgments. AI companies could make these expectations concrete now.

First, they should transform minimalist complaint and redress mechanisms in order to identify widespread harms, including privacy violations, psychological manipulation, and refusals that constrict the free flow of information. In addressing the need for grievance procedures, UNGPs recognize that patterns of complaints can expose systemic problems.

Consider how social media complaint systems centered on takedowns of individual pieces of content failed to adequately address wider concerns about disinformation, polarization, and youth mental health. AI companies should publish regular, detailed accounts of concerns raised about their products, including the nature and frequency of complaints, whether allegations were substantiated, and what corrective measures followed. Independent researchers, red-teamers, and civil society organizations should have formal channels to submit findings and receive substantive responses.

Second, companies should invest substantially in independent scrutiny. Human rights accountability has always depended on rigorous investigation, reporting, and advocacy by independent watchdogs. There is a necessary feedback loop between those shouldering responsibilities and those holding their feet to the fire. Governments themselves fund the U.N.’s human rights machinery, including independent experts who investigate and criticize their conduct.

FP Collections: Download must-read articles on the convergence of artificial intelligence and geopolitics. By FP Contributors.

Recent findings suggest that AI companies should accept a comparable responsibility. Understanding AI demands sophisticated, labor-intensive research on a global scale; the funding to enable that will not materialize without substantial contributions from the companies themselves. They should devote a meaningful share of their growing philanthropic investments to unrestricted, multiyear grants for qualified AI safety, ethics, and human rights organizations.

In a recent development, financial support must be accompanied by access to evidence. Independent researchers need to examine how training datasets are assembled, how models are evaluated and modified, and how external actors might manipulate the information on which AI-generated answers depend. Companies should establish broad, durable access arrangements for qualified researchers, with safeguards for privacy and security. Meta’s discontinuation of CrowdTangle in 2024 and the shuttering of the Stanford Internet Observatory demonstrated how vulnerable independent scrutiny can be to corporate decisions and political pressure.

It has been revealed that A further commitment should concern companies’ relationships with governments, a nexus where some of AI’s gravest threats to rights may arise. Social media companies publish transparency reports on government demands for user data and content removal. Google goes further, disclosing the alleged legal grounds for takedown requests and sharing some actual notices with an independent research database.

Frontier AI companies’ disclosures remain rudimentary. AI developers should report when governments seek access to consumers’ conversations, demand restrictions or changes to model outputs, or request surveillance capabilities. Transparency should also expose the influence that companies exert on governments. The UNGPs specifically cite lobbying as an area where human rights commitments should guide corporate conduct. Microsoft and Google disclose lobbying expenditures and major trade association memberships.

AI companies could go further, identifying the laws and policies that they seek to influence, the organizations that they finance, and how their advocacy comports with their human rights commitments. If they are adhering to their public professions of ethical conduct and public spiritedness, such disclosures should only reinforce their bona fides.

Industry observers note that even the existential risks associated with advanced AI fit within the framework’s logic. The Ruggie principles direct companies to prioritize preventing harms that are severe, widespread, or impossible to remedy. Risks of AI-enabled mass destruction, catastrophic infrastructure failures, or the loss of human control would demand exceptional precautions.

In a recent development, the framework prescribes no tolerable risk threshold but specifies that decisions that could imperil entire populations cannot rest on individual corporate judgments. They require independent evidence, public accountability, and safeguards commensurate with the potential consequences.

Governments could give the Ruggie principles greater force by drawing on established approaches to product safety and corporate accountability. Automobile manufacturers must report consumer complaints, injuries, and potential defects to federal regulators, allowing patterns to emerge that may prompt investigations or recalls. AI developers could face comparable reporting requirements for harmful outputs, recurring failures, and rights violations.

The EU AI Act already takes crucial steps in this direction, requiring developers of the most powerful models to evaluate systemic risks and report serious incidents while empowering regulators to demand information and order corrective measures or withdrawal. California’s frontier AI transparency law, which took effect in 2026, likewise mandates reporting of critical safety incidents and protects employees who raise safety concerns.

In a recent development, the human rights movement arose from the recognition that immense power, exercised without regard for the dignity and rights of the individual, could bring catastrophe. The companies developing artificial intelligence possess extraordinary capabilities, but they need not invent from scratch the principles by which their power should be judged and constrained. Those principles exist. The challenge is to give them force.

Suzanne Nossel is a columnist at Foreign Policy, the Lester Crown senior fellow for U.S. foreign policy and international order at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, and a senior advisor to the Starling Institute. She is the author of Dare to Speak: Defending Free Speech for All. X: @SuzanneNossel.

#42098. China’s AI Diplomacy Is Working

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2472 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

China’s AI Diplomacy Is Working

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2472 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that DANIEL REMLER is a Senior Fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
  • Can the United States and China simultaneously cooperate and compete on AI?
  • Beijing has long appreciated this dynamic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that DANIEL REMLER is a Senior Fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security. He served as AI Policy Coordinator in the Office of the Special Envoy for Critical and Emerging Technology at the State Department from 2023 to 2025.

And America Should Be Taking Notes.

Can the United States and China simultaneously cooperate and compete on AI? That is the question driving debates in Washington about the wisdom of pursuing talks on the subject with Beijing. The Biden administration paired sweeping technology restrictions with a narrow dialogue on risk, and the Trump administration has kept a channel open even as it has downplayed safety. Some experts go further. They hope that cooperation on safety can be siloed off from competition entirely, a belief as appealing as it is fanciful. Any dialogue on AI risk takes place within the broader strategic competition between the United States and China.

Beijing has long appreciated this dynamic. Much of Washington has not. Whereas the United States has shifted its approach to AI competition and safety across and within presidential administrations, Beijing has kept its AI diplomacy focused on gaining competitive advantage over the United States. China has taken part in international AI safety discussions, but it has used them, along with talks with the United States, to paint U.S. export controls as the main obstacle to cooperation. It has cast itself as the champion of the developing world, promising a Chinese-led AI ecosystem without technological or financial barriers as an alternative to a restrictive U.S.-led AI order. The pitch is working. A growing number of states are embracing China’s message, and Chinese open-weight models are gaining consumers across the developing world.

If the United States wants to maintain its lead and make meaningful progress on safety, it needs to treat the dialogue as part of the competition with China. To do so, it must ramp up pressure on China outside the talks and offer countries still choosing sides a more compelling vision for AI adoption and governance. And when U.S. and Chinese officials next meet, in November, Washington should test Beijing’s seriousness about safety. In short, the United States should approach AI diplomacy with the same strategic clarity China has.

The Biden administration’s first round of advanced semiconductor export controls in October 2022 and the release of ChatGPT a month later signaled that the United States had taken an early lead in the AI competition and would act to weaken China’s AI industry. Washington and its allies also seized the diplomatic initiative, taking the first steps toward global AI governance. In May 2023, the G-7 began intense discussions on AI governance that would eventually produce a code of conduct for developers. Weeks later, the United Kingdom unveiled it would host the first global AI safety summit at Bletchley Park.

China responded by rolling out a diplomatic script it has been honing ever since. Its core tenets first appeared in the Global AI Governance Initiative, published in October 2023. It called for countries to “put equal emphasis on development and security” (though it left security to be defined by individual states) and contrasted China’s focus on cooperation and development with U.S. export controls, attacking Washington for “creating barriers and disrupting the global AI supply chain through technological monopolies and unilateral coercive measures.” Despite Beijing’s growing body of AI regulations at home, the initiative offered little more than slogans on the technology’s risks.

That basic formula—cooperation and development, set against U.S. restrictions, with little to say about risk—has guided China’s AI diplomacy for the last three years. In March 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted a U.S.-led resolution on safe, secure, and trustworthy AI intended to appeal to both developed and developing countries. China supported the resolution, then introduced another resolution centered on help for poorer countries and “emphasizing that member states should enjoy equal opportunities” to develop and use AI. At a UN Security Council meeting on AI chaired by the United States in December that year, China’s UN ambassador, Fu Cong, once again counterposed Beijing’s stated interest in cooperation against “discriminatory barriers based on ideological differences.” In thinly veiled terms, Fu was charging that U.S. restrictions on China harmed the developing world.

To win the support of these countries as they built out their AI infrastructure, China needed a bloc of its own. In July 2025, Premier Li Qiang proposed the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), which promised developing countries technology, training, and a greater say in writing global AI rules. In a speech marking its launch a year later, Chinese leader Xi Jinping called for “openness,” shorthand for access to U.S. chips and the adoption of Chinese open-weight models. After urging countries to take the risks of AI seriously, Xi added that they should, “in the meantime,” jointly oppose “overstretching the national security concept in the field of AI and placing one country’s security over that of others.” Cooperation on risks, in Xi’s telling, was subordinate to overcoming U.S. restrictions.

In a recent development, WAICO has promptly gained standing among its target audience. An early endorsement by UN Secretary-General António Guterres lent it immediate credibility in the eyes of developing countries, and Chinese officials have since promoted WAICO in frequent speeches and in bilateral meetings with countries as varied as Brazil, Pakistan, and Serbia. Beijing has signaled that membership will come with perks. Its draft export controls on leading models, released in October, promise to help WAICO’s 37 members build their AI capabilities, suggesting members could have easier access to models restricted for the rest of the world.

It has been revealed that xi personally led this diplomatic offensive in the lead-up to the Washington summit with U.S. President Donald Trump in September. During a speech in Kyrgyzstan, he pledged to expand a Chinese AI center for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization that helps members build local language models and train engineers. In Cairo, he and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi signed agreements on AI, data centers, and semiconductors, which have become a staple of Xi’s trips abroad. And in Upcoming Delhi, Xi proposed an open-source AI zone for BRICS members and told other leaders that a “small yard, high fences” approach would only “box oneself in and divide the world.” AI risks were nowhere on the agenda. The message instead was that U.S. restrictions would isolate Washington, not Beijing.

Recent findings suggest that much of the allure of China’s pitch rests on how the country’s developers share their technology. Chinese developers release their best models with open weights, which any government or tech giant can download, run on its own hardware, and adapt to its own language. For governments wary of depending on American companies whose exports Washington can restrict, open-weight models promise a greater degree of control. Chinese developers rarely conduct or publish the results of any safety testing for these models, leaving others to discover after release whether, for example, they can be used to launch cyberattacks or build weapons. But their accessibility allows Beijing to argue that any effort to contain the risks of Chinese models is an attempt to deny AI to the developing world.

China’s approach to bilateral AI talks with the United States has deflected discussions of risk just as assiduously as its global AI diplomacy has. In May 2024, the United States and China held talks in Geneva, which I joined as part of the U.S. delegation. The U.S. objective of the talks was to test whether an in-depth technical exchange with China on AI risk was possible. The answer was no. Chinese diplomats steered the discussion away from risks for hours and declined to even explain China’s own AI regulations beyond a superficial overview, despite having technical experts from the relevant agencies in the room.

Industry observers note that the Chinese position came through most clearly in the opening and closing remarks of the delegation’s most senior officials. They began with an appeal for cooperation on capacity-building projects in the developing world. They then cast U.S. technology restrictions as an attempt to contain China’s development and the U.S. emphasis on safety as a barrier preventing developing countries from accessing and using AI. The implication was clear—export controls were the primary impediment to cooperation on AI safety. The one concrete outcome, a November 2024 statement in which former President Joe Biden and Xi affirmed “the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons,” asked little of Beijing.

This September, after the summit between Trump and Xi in Washington, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs published an “eight-point consensus,” Beijing’s account of what the two sides had agreed to. It described the dialogue as an exchange on the “risks and benefits” of AI. But whereas the White House framed the dialogue as a security problem, listing it alongside nuclear arms control, China’s Ministry of Commerce stressed instead that talks had taken place, and would continue, under the two countries’ economic and trade mechanism. Folded into trade talks, a dialogue on AI risks and benefits leaves Beijing free to parry U.S. requests on risks, such as limits on openly releasing models with dangerous capabilities, by demanding that Washington relax export controls.

Recent findings suggest that xi did propose to “jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI,” conveniently eliding China’s own frequent use of AI against the United States in various ways, such as hacking campaigns and influence operations. He added that AI should remain under human control and be developed for good, a principle Beijing has repeated since 2023 but about which it has offered little further detail or follow-through. More pointed was his insistence that future dialogue should “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other” and his request that Chinese companies be “treated fairly,” both implicit rebukes of U.S. restrictions.

In a recent development, this record suggests Beijing will come to future meetings, beginning with the next discussion in November, with proposals designed to put Washington in a bind. Although U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has made clear that export controls are not on the table, Beijing will raise them anyway. If Washington engages, Chinese negotiators will claim a standing channel where U.S. restrictions on AI technology are up for negotiation. If it refuses, Beijing will continue to evade U.S. entreaties on safety while accusing Washington of stifling opportunity for developing countries. It hopes that every round of the dialogue will further cement an impression among allies such as Japan and the Netherlands that Washington will trade away restrictions over their heads, and that they should accommodate China’s AI ambitions, too.

But Washington is in a stronger position than its diplomacy has let on. The world’s leading models are still American, and, together with allies, the United States controls key chokepoints in the semiconductor supply chain. Export controls on those chokepoints are not a bargaining chip and should be strengthened. Chinese AI companies regularly lament their lack of high-end chips and have resorted to smuggling chips and illicitly distilling U.S. models. U.S. developers also conduct increasingly extensive and transparent safety testing, which Chinese developers avoid. Taken together, these strengths give Washington the means to press Beijing and an attractive offer for the rest of the world. It should use them, advertising its rigorously tested models to compete for global adoption while pressuring China on safety in the dialogue.

In a recent development, the first chance to apply that pressure is the next bilateral meeting. Washington should set two conditions for it and future meetings. Chinese developers must commit to publishing safety evaluations at least as extensive as those that leading U.S. developers publish today on equivalent benchmarks for the most serious risks, such as cyberattacks and biological weapons, and to disclosing previous and future incidents. The United States can make the same commitments, as its companies already publish such evaluations, increasingly disclose incidents, and open their models to independent and government evaluators before release. Otherwise, the incident channel to which the two sides agreed in September will run one way, with China free to point to U.S. incidents while reporting none of its own.

It has been revealed that these conditions would change the terms of the dialogue. Since 2023, Washington has raised risks and Beijing has steered the conversation toward development. As long as Chinese companies face no scrutiny for the risks of their models, Beijing can tout them for their openness and innovation without having to answer questions from the rest of the world about their safety. Concordia AI, which tracks China’s AI ecosystem, found that only five of China’s ten leading developers published safety test results for any model over the past year, and none did so consistently. If China agrees, governments and companies choosing which models to use will be able to judge Chinese and American developers by the same criteria. If China refuses, the onus will be on Beijing to explain why fair treatment for Chinese companies should not extend to safety testing. Regardless, the U.S. government should ramp up its own tests of new Chinese models and publish the results. It should also avoid unforced errors, such as Trump’s waving away of AI safety concerns as a “hoax,” which hand Beijing an easy retort to U.S. appeals.

Sources indicate that more broadly, effective AI diplomacy ultimately requires convincing other countries to join the American AI ecosystem. Countries that train their engineers, build their local language models, and run their data centers on Chinese technology will come to depend on it. To counter that dependence (and prevent it from turning into political alignment), Washington needs to present a positive vision of AI governance that pairs verifiable safety commitments—the kind Chinese developers avoid—with the access and investment developing countries want.

U.S. companies already offer the best technology, but Washington has yet to put real diplomatic weight behind them. It should draw from its evolving approach at home to rally partners around shared safety measures. Under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed in September, six leading U.S. companies committed themselves to internal controls, external audits, and independent oversight. The G-7 Code of Conduct, which built on voluntary commitments secured under the Biden administration, could incorporate the accord’s measures and serve as a common standard for partners. Countries that agree to its measures could receive priority for technology and financing. Without such incentives, the AI competition may be determined by price and access alone, where China has the edge.

Much of Washington has treated talks with Beijing as a place to manage the shared risks of AI apart from the competition. China has always treated them as an arena of the larger rivalry. To maintain its lead and make real progress on safety, the United States should start doing the same.

According to recent reports, as Russia’s war in Ukraine grinds on, to travel around Europe is often to be confronted with apocalyptic warnings. Europe and Russia are “closer now to all-out war” than at any moment since the Cuban missile crisis, Russian exile Alexander Meniukov told me at a subway station cafe in central Warsaw, Poland. “The Soviet regime was pragmatic. Sources indicate that as Russia’s war in Ukraine grinds on, to travel around Europe is often to be confronted with apocalyptic warnings. Europe and Russia are “closer now to all-out war” than at any moment since the Cuban missile crisis, Russian exile Alexander Meniukov told me at a subway station cafe in central Warsaw, Poland. “The Soviet regime was pragmatic. Putin is emotional,” he mentioned. In a hotel room in Tallinn, Estonia, I watched a news report about Romanian troops running urban combat drills on the streets of Bucharest.

European governments take seriously the prospect of war with Russia. Across the continent, defense budgets have swelled as countries rush to rearm. In 2026 alone, the European Union’s 27 member states will spend a combined 454 billion euros on their defense capacities—an 8.6 percent increase over last year’s expenditure, which marked a post-Cold War peak.

It has been revealed that but as this spending intensifies, centrist lawmakers and their allies are overlooking the potential political pitfalls. This is particularly true in countries that have seemingly sacrificed other government programs on the altar of security.

Recent findings suggest that germany is a case in point. In April, Chancellor Friedrich Merz unveiled cuts to the country’s social infrastructure totaling 38.3 billion euros over the next three years. Merz has spoken often about what he sees as the necessity of streamlining Germany’s social safety net. “The welfare state that we have today can no longer be financed with what we produce in the economy,” he told a gathering of his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) colleagues last year.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Merz has overseen a massive increase in German military expenditure, spooked by the cumulative shock of Russia’s revanchist campaign in Ukraine and U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to the White House. By 2030, Germany’s total defense outlays will hit 183.7 billion euros, one-fifth of the federal budget. Merz’s goal, widely shared across the German political spectrum, is to turn the country’s military into the most formidable fighting force in Europe by the late 2030s.

It has been revealed that the United Kingdom is making similar trade-offs. In June, shortly before he was ousted as prime minister, Keir Starmer published a newly introduced “Defence Investment Initiative.” If implemented, the plan will increase British government spending on core defense requirements from 2.3 percent of GDP to 2.7 percent by 2029 and then to 3.5 percent by 2035, in line with NATO mandates. This will be supported by 15 billion pounds of additional defense spending in the next four years, 7 billion pounds of which will be funded by cuts to the budgets of other departments.

Sources indicate that starmer acknowledged in June that the net effect of these cuts would be scrapping certain infrastructure projects and net-zero initiatives across the U.K. Notably, new Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who otherwise tends to sit to Starmer’s left, has largely accepted the plan’s recommendations.

As tensions with Russia rise, these sums are only likely to grow. Senior European Union policymakers cast the continent’s security as a choice between social democracy and outstripping Russia’s massive defense spending. “Member states collectively spent an average 1.9 percent of GDP on defense,” Kaja Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs, noted in a speech in Brussels last year. “Russia is spending 9 percent. We spend billions on our schools, healthcare, and welfare, but if we don’t invest more in defense, all of this is at risk.”.

In the U.K., a cross-party coalition ranging from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to former Labour member of Parliament and NATO Secretary-General George Robertson has urged the government to implement harsher fiscal measures to fund the country’s ever-inflating defense brief. “We must cut welfare to fund our defense,” Badenoch stated in August. “We must.”.

It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that such figures have lost sight of political realities. The most obvious is that across Europe, but particularly in Germany and the U.K., the far right is on the rise. According to the latest polls, Alternative for Germany (AfD) sits 10 points ahead of Merz’s CDU at the federal level. Meanwhile, Nigel Farage’s post-Brexit Reform UK party is in second, six points behind the Labour party—despite being hit by a string of financial scandals in recent months. The popularity of European far-right parties has been growing since the 2008 financial crisis; the trend is likely to accelerate with a fresh round of fiscal retrenchment.

In a recent development, the evidence that cutting investment in public services bolsters support for far-right and anti-establishment movements seems more than just anecdotal. Thiemo Fetzer’s widely cited 2020 paper found a clear and “causal link between individual-or-regional-level exposure to austerity and support for Leave” in the 2016 Brexit vote, tracing the political impact of the deficit reduction policies between 2010 and 2015. At the time, both Conservative and Labour leaders argued that cuts were necessary, but they entailed massive reductions to local budgets—and an accompanying explosion in poverty rates in the regions where support for Leave was strongest.

In Germany, the Agenda 2010 reforms implemented by the Social Democratic Party (SPD) between 2003 and 2005 slashed unemployment payments and significantly raised the number of Germans in low-paid work. Part of Chancellor Gerhard Schröder’s drive to reinvigorate the economy, the reforms ultimately eroded support for the SPD and opened a political vacuum. A decade later, it has been filled by the socialist Left party and the AfD on the radical right. The AfD is the second-largest party in the Bundestag and the most popular party in the five states that make up former East Germany. Support for the SPD is at historic lows.

Both AfD co-leader Alice Weidel and Farage have been critical of Western support for Ukraine in the past and urged a more conciliatory approach toward Russia. Weidel flatly opposes further German military assistance to Ukraine and has described Kyiv’s prospective NATO membership as “completely unacceptable.” What Weidel and Farage would do if they held power is anyone’s guess. General elections in both Germany and the U.K. are due in or before 2029.

The political folly of the warfare-versus-welfare paradigm is underscored by the fact that European voters at large, exhausted by years of inflation, stagnant wages, and rising energy costs, are not keen on paying for rearmament via further attrition of their living standards. “A large majority of [Europeans] tend to disagree with any option of welfare cutbacks proposed to increase military spending,” a detailed analysis of Europe-wide polling in the Journal of European Policy concluded this year.

Industry observers note that the ongoing civil unrest in France, which started as a student-led protest against the country’s strained education system and expanded into a wider revolt over inequality and the cost of living, shows how far working-class Europeans are prepared to go to protect what remains of postwar welfare provision. In Spain, where elections loom on Nov. 29, students and trade unionists are leading a street campaign for more affordable housing; Italy, too, has seen mass protests over rising costs. Germany and the U.K. could be next. With uniquely poor timing given the urgency of the risk posed by Russia, Europe looks increasingly distracted and divided.

Sources indicate that A further irony is that, at least in the short term, remilitarization means European states purchasing more U.S. weapons, deepening their military dependence on an unreliable partner. Under pressure from Trump, who has repeatedly dangled the threat of a U.S. withdrawal from NATO, Europe has significantly increased its volume of arms purchases from the United States. Prior to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Europe was already reliant on U.S. Patriot missiles for its security. European arms imports from the United States have since roughly doubled.

According to recent reports, trump’s hostility toward NATO is built on the crude belief that Europeans have been spending lavishly at the United States’ expense since the end of the Cold War. Trump has dispatched top U.S. officials, including Vice President J.D. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to Europe in the last 18 months to hammer home the message that, from Washington’s perspective, the era of this so-called European peace dividend is over.

Yet for ordinary Europeans, the end of the Cold War didn’t necessarily generate the perks that Trump imagines. After 1991, most European countries did shrink their defense budgets. But the subsequent fiscal savings mostly weren’t spent on generous unemployment benefits or working-class wages. They were spent either on basic governmental support, such as healthcare and state pensions, or on tax cuts for corporate executives and the ultra-rich.

In a recent development, “From the mid-1980s to 2023, corporate income tax rates fell by around half within [OECD countries],” Shahin Vallée and Joseph de Weck of the German Council for Foreign Relations wrote recently. “Social protection for the working age population has fallen across Europe since the end of the cold war.”.

None of this means that Europe should not be able to defend itself against Russia, if and when a confrontation arrives; rearmament may be necessary. But it would be foolish for Europe to rearm in a way that punishes ordinary people. It is increasingly clear that the political risks of rearmament are being missed as Russian belligerence grows, the specter of U.S. isolationism intensifies, and European nerves fray.

Welfare austerity is not the only option. Governments could borrow more to bolster their defenses—or they could impose a defense tax on their richest citizens, circumventing the need to scorch front-line services. The sense of panic in Europe is real and rising, but panic does not make for good policy.

The leaders of the United States, Russia and China gathered in Shenzhen for historic three-way talks, emphasizing the importance of continued diplomacy and maintaining open dialogue despite longstanding differences.

President Donald Trump joined the leaders of China and Russia Thursday for an unprecedented three-way summit, marking a historic moment in global diplomacy as the three powers discussed nuclear arms reductions, the war in Ukraine and global security without announcing a major breakthrough.

The unprecedented three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin underscored the leaders' commitment to continued diplomacy, with Trump emphasizing the importance of maintaining dialogue among rival nuclear powers.

It has been revealed that trump left the trilateral meeting, which lasted more than an hour, around 5 a.m. ET and headed to the airport. He is not expected to deliver public remarks before flying back to Washington, Fox News reported.

"We are really making history," Trump declared during the meeting in Shenzhen, China, as he sought to cast the gathering itself as a diplomatic achievement.

It has been revealed that the three leaders are meeting on the sidelines of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by China from November 18–19. (Win McNamee/Getty Images).

The three leaders sat down at a roundtable just after 3 a.m. ET, roughly two hours behind schedule.

Trump argued that bringing the three leaders together offered an opportunity to address problems that had long divided their countries.

Sources indicate that "Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," Trump stated. "But no problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them.".

"Together we are choosing a different course," he added.

Ahead of the summit, Trump told Fox News' Jacqui Heinrich that he wanted to meet with Xi and Putin together "because they work together, they have a relationship.".

In a recent development, trump argued that previous U.S. policies had helped bring Moscow and Beijing closer together, despite their historically strained relationship.

"They were natural enemies, but because of Obama, not Biden, it was Obama before he drove them together because of energy," Trump mentioned.

Russia and China had a fractured relationship for decades following their split in the 1960s, but energy ties deepened through a major 2014 gas deal signed during Obama's presidency after roughly a decade of negotiations.

In a recent development, president Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin attend a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on November 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. (Win McNamee/Getty Images).

It has been revealed that xi, who hosted the gathering, called the meeting a "groundbreaking move" and stressed the responsibility of the three powers to maintain global stability. However, no substantial breakthroughs were immediately announced.

"Our positive interaction is not optional, but a must," Xi stated through a translator, arguing that the countries must work together to confront global challenges and preserve international peace.

Putin similarly emphasized the countries' shared responsibility for international security, pointing to their status as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council before turning to one of the summit's most pressing issues: the war in Ukraine.

"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including, obviously, the conflict in Ukraine," Putin mentioned through a translator.

"I think things are happening," Trump remarked. "I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war.".

Sources indicate that the historic summit followed separate meetings between Trump and the two leaders. Trump met with Putin for approximately 40 minutes before holding a meeting with Xi that lasted more than an hour.

The president also raised the possibility of broader nuclear arms reductions while acknowledging the difficulty of persuading nuclear-armed nations to surrender their weapons.

"It's a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them," Trump said.

It has been revealed that president Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images).

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of complications even as he appears politically weakened at home.

According to recent reports, trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

Sources indicate that the U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, mentioned Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he remarked. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”.

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., noted part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” noted Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

Sources indicate that “I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump stated Monday. “I think he's backing down.”.

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a major reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, mentioned he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”.

Sources indicate that “I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”.

Sources indicate that during remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

In a recent development, “Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he noted. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”.

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

Sources indicate that he stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, remarked Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”.

Recent findings suggest that trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the firm’s president and CEO. He also mentioned he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

According to recent reports, the administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”.

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”.

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear concerns dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”.

Breaking: Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea
