Industry News: The World’s Last Chance for Peace

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.
  • At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable.
  • Nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.

At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable. Wars of aggression, from Ukraine to Lebanon to Iran, are on the rise, bringing horror, ruin, and the specter of a wider international confrontation. Governments increasingly treat war as something to budget and prepare for. Military spending is climbing, technological and arms races are intensifying, and more and more countries are considering whether they should acquire a nuclear deterrent to guarantee their security.

Nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war. It represents a return to a norm that persisted for most of human history, when war was the main organizing principle of the international system. Armed conflict was the natural way for states to settle disputes or enlarge their territory at the expense of weaker neighbors.

Industry observers note that yet the vast wreckage of World Wars I and II in the first half of the twentieth century made the status quo unacceptable. Countries united behind an effort to turn war from a legitimate instrument of statecraft into an outlawed act. Wars did not end in 1945, but for years after they were overwhelmingly condemned by the international community.

Sources indicate that in recent decades, however, governments’ commitment to the cause of peace has weakened. Millions of people took to the streets in hundreds of cities to oppose the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, but the war proceeded nonetheless. Fought on false premises and in violation of international law, it brought destruction to Iraq, fed regional instability, and fueled resentment and terrorism directed at Western countries. The conflict also marked a turning point. Ever since, the pursuit of peace has steadily receded from the international agenda amid deepening geopolitical competition and inattention or indifference to the multilateral efforts that for decades discouraged acts of war.

At the end of this path lies another world war—the catastrophe the twentieth-century order was designed to prevent. With that dire future looming, governments must relearn the art of opposing war. It is the responsibility of every country, including my own, Spain, to take direct action that constrains others’ ability to wage war and to strengthen the international institutions that will serve as guarantors of peace.

It has been revealed that the success of this project will depend on an expansive multilateralism that I call “maxilateralism”—cooperation that embraces as many countries as possible, rather than being limited to small, ad hoc groupings. Its ambition is to make war increasingly impractical, even unimaginable. In 2003, protesters across Spain chanted “No a la guerra!’’—“No to war!” The world cannot afford to ignore them again.

International efforts to reject war as an instrument of national policy date back to the Kellogg–Briand Pact of 1928, a treaty signed in Paris by 15 countries and joined by dozens more later. It was insufficient to prevent World War II, but it planted a seed. When representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to create the United Nations, they revived the spirit and principles of Kellogg–Briand and gave them what they had lacked: institutional form. The UN Charter prohibited the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. And, unlike its 1928 predecessor, it backed up the prohibition with institutions empowered to enforce it.

Industry observers note that in the decades that followed, these institutions established an order that penalized violations and created incentives for diplomacy and cooperation. At the same time, public opposition to war was growing stronger around the world. Popular defiance of Cold War militarism was visible in worldwide resistance to the Vietnam War and in mass movements against nuclear weapons. Pacifism reached its high-water mark in the 1990s, when a vibrant global civil society mobilized to defend humanitarian causes and when the United Nations held sufficient authority to champion a sweeping peace agenda.

According to recent reports, today, however, there is more armed conflict than at any time since 1946. According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010. An estimated 250,000 people died in those conflicts—the highest annual death toll in 30 years, since the Rwandan genocide. Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war.

Worryingly, wars of aggression—which violate the UN Charter—are back. Russia invaded Ukraine. The United States and Israel attacked Iran. And as fighting continues year after year in places such as Lebanon, Sudan, and Yemen, it is becoming clear that war is being accepted as a normal occurrence.

There is no sign of the trend slowing down. Military budgets have surged to levels not seen in generations, at the expense of social and development spending. In the past decade alone, global defense spending has increased by more than 40 percent, with many countries doubling their military budgets. The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent. Even countries with a long tradition of military restraint, such as Denmark, Germany, Japan, and Norway, are rearming rapidly. Some are reviving military service programs.

It has been revealed that A renewed threat of nuclear war is cause for still greater dread. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, boosting their destructive capabilities. China’s nuclear arsenal is estimated to have increased from 200 to 300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 this year. North Korea has also expanded its arsenal from an estimated ten to 20 warheads in 2018 to around 60 this year, and it has developed increasingly sophisticated launch platforms. In March, France announced the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992. The United States and Russia, the world’s two largest nuclear powers, have failed to preserve the last remaining treaty constraining their strategic arsenals. And a growing number of nonnuclear powers have started to consider acquiring arsenals of their own.

In a recent development, simultaneously, artificial intelligence is powering ever more dangerous weapons of war. Human oversight is being progressively reduced as AI makes it possible to automate cyberattacks against power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. AI systems have hacked government bodies and enabled the mass production of deepfakes and disinformation campaigns.

The integration of AI into nuclear technologies poses an existential threat: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment. Similarly, the use of AI in biotechnology could dramatically lower barriers to harmful experimentation and the development of bioweapons. In both areas, this technology is elevating the risk of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and mass destruction to a level higher than ever before.

In a recent development, together, these dynamics are multiplying the chances that any crisis will rapidly spiral into planetary annihilation. Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation while the instruments of control move at the much slower pace of diplomacy.

Recent findings suggest that political change is pushing the world away from peace and toward confrontation and militarization. A multipolar world is not, by definition, a more dangerous one, but the erosion of rules and institutions that manage tensions between poles has made today’s world particularly volatile. Competition among great powers is increasing, with hegemonic ambitions encouraging assertive foreign policies and revisionist states challenging established rules and borders. Belligerent nationalism is on the rise, and far-right movements are advancing a worldview in which international relations is a zero-sum game and countries must compete rather than cooperate. Even centrist leaders are embracing the language of war preparedness. Although they do not intend to start a war, their words feed a dangerous militaristic mindset.

In this context of rivalry, wars of aggression come wrapped in narratives of necessity, liberation, self-defense, or historical justice. The attackers present their operations as inevitable, having demonized their targets to justify preemptive action against them. They describe each war as an answer to insecurity—a war to end all wars.

Sources indicate that but these wars will not make a safer world. Every time a state embarks on a war of aggression, it erodes the norms that protect all countries from the arbitrary use of force—including the aggressor itself.

In a recent development, wars exact immense costs. They shatter societies and interrupt lives. In 2025, at least one civilian died in an armed conflict every 14 minutes, according to UN records, and more than five million people were forced to flee their countries. The economic costs are high, too; the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities, and millions of people across the world are suffering the consequences.

Industry observers note that war also creates upcoming dangers. Once the fighting begins, its course is unpredictable. Conflict tends to draw in new actors and spill into neighboring countries. The war in Iran serves, again, as a prime example. Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors—actions Spain has consistently condemned. Attacks on civilian and commercial vessels threaten broader regional stability. And the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen.

Finally, wars rarely produce lasting peace. Instead, they deepen grievances and entrench divisions that fuel future violence. Russia’s war in Ukraine, for instance, has destroyed trust in Moscow. The genocide in Gaza has inflamed anger toward Israel, potentially leading to new waves of terrorism. And the war against Iran has further destabilized the Middle East, hindering cooperation across the region.

According to recent reports, the world has a responsibility to resist the normalization of wars. Remaining silent is an act of cowardice and complicity. Spanish society is making its position clear: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater number believe another world war is on the horizon.

But it is not enough to simply condemn war in principle. The ambition of ending war must be matched with action that makes it increasingly difficult for countries to start, sustain, and justify armed conflict.

Spain has endeavored to take such action. It has defended the international laws that stand between an order governed by rules and one governed by force. Spain has consistently denounced armed attacks that violate the UN Charter.

From day one of the war in Gaza, Spain has been calling for an immediate and permanent cease-fire, the release of all hostages, and the unrestricted delivery of humanitarian assistance. In May 2024, Spain recognized the state of Palestine in the hope that this step would help advance a negotiated and lasting solution to the conflict. And Spain has actively supported the efforts of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court to hold Israeli leaders accountable for violations of international humanitarian law. Israel had the right to self-defense after the October 7 terrorist attacks, but that right does not justify genocide in Gaza or the expansion of Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.

Deterring war also requires raising the costs of aggression. The rest of the world must ensure that those who choose to wage war cannot do so without paying a price. Throughout Russia’s war in Ukraine, for example, the European Union has introduced a series of sanctions on Russia, which Spain has consistently supported. Spain has also provided financial, humanitarian, and military assistance to Ukraine, helping it defend its territory and deny Russia the spoils of war.

Countries must refuse to help belligerents expand existing conflicts. Spain, for instance, has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023. This year, it also denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran. Spain’s decision was not an act of hostility toward an ally. Nor was it an expression of neutrality or sympathy for the Iranian regime. It was, rather, a judgment that getting involved would enable escalation of the conflict, deepening regional and global insecurity. To keep its commitment to peace, Spain had to be willing to say no, even when doing so carried a political cost. Had more countries done the same, the wars in Gaza and Iran would have been far harder and costlier to wage.

In a recent development, investing in prosperity is also essential. Security is strengthened when societies are resilient, inequalities are reduced, and citizens can rely on public institutions. Spain’s decision last year to opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP reflected this understanding. This position did not stem from a lack of commitment to European defense—in fact, my government has championed Europe’s push for strategic autonomy and has tripled net defense spending over the eight years I have been in office. But military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other. By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain has preserved the fiscal space to invest an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education, as well as more than 30 billion euros in the green transition—programs that make society more cohesive and adaptable, and therefore more secure.

It has been revealed that yet one country’s efforts can accomplish only so much. Starving war of its lifelines requires all hands on deck, a collective effort rooted in genuine multilateralism. This is the only strategy that has worked before. The multilateral system built after World War II spanned the globe, and it helped keep peace among great powers and prevent a third world war.

Sources indicate that reinforcing it will not be an easy task. Geopolitical competition and widespread mistrust have weakened the United Nations, international financial bodies, regional organizations, and other multilateral institutions. Many countries perceive them as ineffective and trapped in perpetual crisis, so they have turned to alternative frameworks to try to end wars.

In a recent development, some have tried unilateral approaches, pursuing transactional bargains that end up benefiting economic and political elites while sidelining the populations affected by the conflict. The cease-fires or peace deals they achieve may be preferable to continued war, but any peace imposed through power politics rather than law rests on shaky foundations.

In a recent development, other countries, frustrated with multilateralism, have tried recruiting coalitions of the willing, or other “minilateral” groups, to provide security guarantees or reach ad hoc arrangements on matters of trade and technology. This approach might be a temporary solution to the paralysis of traditional institutions, but its exclusivity further fragments an already divided international order. What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism. International cooperation is powerful when it is, or aspires to be, universal. Leaving part of the world outside of multilateral efforts, moreover, is a recipe for confrontation down the road.

According to recent reports, the twentieth-century system was not perfect. The application of its rules has been uneven, its standards inconsistently upheld, its procedures frustratingly slow. But it is undeniable that the world would be much more dangerous without it. To take just one example, it was a lattice of international treaties—including the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the Limited Test Ban Treaty—that ended a wildly expensive arms race that was driving the world to the brink of nuclear war.

All of this institutional architecture is now eroding. Yet without it, the world cannot aspire to preserve peace.

Strengthening multilateral institutions must be at the center of a global campaign to relegate war to history. This will require substantial reform to restore these institutions’ legitimacy and their capacity to act, prioritizing measures that will contribute the most to peace and security.

The first is increasing representation at the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions. An patch to the structure of the UN Security Council is particularly crucial, given that body’s primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace. A Security Council that gives permanent seats and a right to veto only to the five victors of World War II, which together account for barely a quarter of the global population, does not reflect today’s world. The council’s elected membership should be expanded and the terms of those members should be extended beyond the current two years. The fresh seats should be given primarily to countries in underrepresented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. Regional organizations such as the European Union and the African Union should also be represented in the council, potentially taking over seats right now occupied by states. A more representative Security Council would not merely be fairer; it would also be more effective. Countries are more likely to defend and enforce international rules when they consider themselves to be authors of those rules.

Permanent members’ veto power must also be strictly limited, particularly when the Security Council considers cases of mass atrocities, genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright. Only then can the council respond to all acts of aggression without being paralyzed by the objections of a single state.

A similar spirit should guide structural change at international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The distribution of voting power in both still reflects twentieth-century economic balances, and by convention, a European always leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank. This must end. Emerging economies need better representation, and leadership positions should be open to all candidates regardless of nationality. Responsibilities within institutions such as the World Trade Organization should also evolve as economic growth moves countries that were once categorized as “developing” into the ranks of the wealthy. Fairer economic governance would ease the inequality and resentment that so often feed instability and conflict.

Another key reform will involve reinvigorating the international framework that limits the risk of nuclear escalation. Some of that work depends on the nuclear powers; it is up to the United States and Russia, for example, to negotiate a successor to the bilateral Latest START treaty that preserves verifiable limits on strategic nuclear deployments. And this time, China should be part of the discussions.

Recent findings suggest that yet the broader effort requires the engagement of all countries. Their priorities should include ratifying the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to prevent a resumption of nuclear testing and advancing negotiations on a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, which would ban production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for nuclear weapons. All countries must also work together to regulate the use of AI in the military domain, especially when it comes to nuclear weapons, to preserve human control over launch decisions and reduce the risk of catastrophic errors. Nonnuclear powers should commit to not acquiring nuclear weapons themselves, and they should use every tool at their disposal to encourage nuclear powers to reduce their arsenals, strengthen verification mechanisms, and rebuild the diplomatic guardrails that for decades have helped prevent nuclear catastrophe.

Technology can help with some of this. Advances in satellite imagery, remote sensors, and data analytics can increase transparency and make compliance with arms control agreements more observable. But more must be done to avoid situations that can escalate into war. If nuclear-armed states agree to lower operational readiness and strengthen crisis communication, that can help ensure that governments have the time and the means to defuse dangerous situations. Each country must protect its command-and-control systems from cyberattacks and AI-driven manipulation of information, so that a false alarm or miscalculation never leads to nuclear war.

It has been revealed that the final priority is to ensure that the international justice system can enforce courts’ decisions. Dismantling the International Criminal Court, as some countries are trying to do, would only ensure that the world’s gravest crimes go unpunished. The ICC should not only prosecute cases of genocide, aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity but also have the authority to bring to justice those who are responsible for these crimes. When a state becomes a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the ICC, it agrees to submit itself to the court’s jurisdiction. Yet if that state refuses to cooperate or surrender a suspect, there is no real punishment, only an embarrassing censure. This must change. States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences. Starting and waging war should carry a real cost.

Proposals to reform international institutions have long struggled to gain traction, but the coming election of a fresh UN secretary-general offers a rare opportunity to inject fresh momentum into these efforts. Were the UN to appoint its first female leader, it would be a powerful symbol of renewal, inclusion, and institutional adaptation. The organization cannot truly claim to speak on behalf of all humanity until it has had a woman leading it. Reaching this milestone could kindle a new sense of ambition and instill greater confidence in the capacity of international institutions to reform themselves—and to reclaim their role in constraining war.

Sources indicate that halting the world’s march toward war will require the broadest possible commitment. All countries, large and small, must refuse to look away or to participate in escalatory action. They must stand by the international norms that constrain war today, and reform and empower the institutions that will make it impossible tomorrow.

Ultimately, what will make war unimaginable is a positive peace agenda that addresses the root causes of insecurity. Every step toward eradicating poverty, expanding access to quality education, advancing gender equality, strengthening democratic institutions, and increasing disaster resilience also eases the conditions that produce violence.

Sources indicate that international financial institutions must be able to deliver financing promptly, at scale, and at reasonable cost, so that no developing country is forced to choose between servicing its debt and investing in its people. Multilateral development banks must be able to mobilize funds for the green and digital transitions, so that climate migration and competition over resources do not become drivers of interstate conflict. And the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement must be finalized and put into force to ensure that all countries will be able to access vaccines and treatments when the next global health emergency strikes.

According to recent reports, this is why Spain has sought to place development at the heart of its foreign policy. The Spanish government has championed the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, and last year the city of Seville hosted the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, where delegates committed to easing the debt burden of vulnerable countries and unlocking investment for sustainable development. Spain has also promoted initiatives such as the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps, launched with the World Bank; the multilateral Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, which allows vulnerable countries to pause debt payments after disasters; and its own mechanism to provide up to 60 million euros in debt relief for developing countries each year. In addition, Spain has backed climate finance, global health, gender equality, food security, and social protection initiatives in partnership with multilateral institutions and international organizations. These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.

A larger project to rally the world behind legal norms and genuine multilateralism may seem unrealistic. But we have seen what happens when the normalization of war drags humanity into hell. The men and women who emerged from the ruins of World War II, the darkest chapter in human history, found a way to construct a multilateral world order. The question before our generation is whether we will preserve the rule of law or allow a return to rule by force. Whether we build the world of tomorrow through foresight and cooperation, or through the chaos and pain of another world war. We must choose wisely while the choice is still ours to make.

ICJ to Deliver Landmark Verdict on Myanmar

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the International Court of Justice (ICJ) is set to deliver a Nov.
  • In a span of roughly two and a half months that year, the Myanmar military killed thousands of people, committed widespread and organized sexual assault, and razed nearly 400 villages in northern Rakhine state.
  • The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is set to deliver a Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Industry observers note that the International Court of Justice (ICJ) is set to deliver a Nov. 19 verdict on whether Myanmar violated the Genocide Convention during the mass persecution and massacres of the Rohingya people that began in August 2017. The ICJ has never found a state responsible for genocide; such a verdict in this case would have immediate and wide-ranging impacts.

In a span of roughly two and a half months that year, the Myanmar military killed thousands of people, committed widespread and organized sexual assault, and razed nearly 400 villages in northern Rakhine state. More than 700,000 Rohingya fled across the Naf River into Bangladesh, where many of them now remain in refugee camps.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is set to deliver a Nov. 19 verdict on whether Myanmar violated the Genocide Convention during the mass persecution and massacres of the Rohingya people that began in August 2017. The ICJ has never found a state responsible for genocide; such a verdict in this case would have immediate and wide-ranging impacts.

In a span of roughly two and a half months that year, the Myanmar military killed thousands of people, committed widespread and organized sexual assault, and razed nearly 400 villages in northern Rakhine state. More than 700,000 Rohingya fled across the Naf River into Bangladesh, where many of them now remain in refugee camps.

Recent findings suggest that for Rohingya victims, the ICJ case presents an opportunity to have their suffering recognized on one of international law’s biggest stages. For opponents of Myanmar’s military regime—which recently rebranded itself as a nominally civilian government—a verdict that finds the state culpable of genocide could serve as a lever to halt the regime’s recent emergence from diplomatic isolation.

Industry observers note that and in the eyes of the global pro-Palestinian movement, it would likely signal a looming genocide verdict for Israel at the same court, although that decision is not expected for a few more years. The Myanmar case is expected to set a number of international legal precedents, including those concerning standards of evidence and reparations.

“From an international law perspective, this case is once in a generation,” noted Michelle Onello, a senior legal advisor at the Global Justice Center, a humanitarian law organization.

Gambia brought the Myanmar case to the ICJ in 2019, marking the first time that the court—which hears disputes between nations—took up a genocide case lodged by a country not directly affected. Gambia argued that Myanmar violated a treaty that both countries are party to, the Genocide Convention. In December 2023, South Africa used the same argument to pursue a genocide case against Israel for its conduct during the Gaza war.

Sources indicate that “In Gaza, the Palestinians were subject to killing and other violence on a scale that considerably exceeds that of Myanmar,” remarked William Schabas, a professor of international law at Middlesex University. Schabas served on Myanmar’s defense team but resigned after the military seized power in 2021. “A finding that Myanmar committed genocide will therefore make a finding that Israel has committed it much more likely.”.

Lucky Karim was just 14 years old when the Myanmar military came to burn her village in Maungdaw township in 2017. “You just keep running until you are told to rest,” she noted of the experience fleeing the village during an interview this month.

It has been revealed that before the escalation in 2017, the Rohingya faced severe restrictions on their freedom of movement in Myanmar, access to healthcare and education, and citizenship status. The situation worsened in 2012, when thousands of people were driven from their homes during sectarian riots and forced into squalid displacement camps.

There were warning signs in the weeks leading up to the 2017 crackdown, Karim stated, including the military arresting people who could read and write in order to leave the rest of the community in darkness. Around a week before the Muslim holiday of Eid al-Adha, the military began raiding Rohingya villages.

“We have experienced this in most of our lives in Myanmar. Right before a significant event for Muslims to celebrate, they will do something terrible,” Karim stated. “But we never thought it was going to be something permanent.” But by the time that her family reached Bangladesh, after a week of walking, her village was a smoldering ruin.

According to recent reports, myanmar’s de facto leader at the time, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, was widely seen as downplaying the atrocities—though she had no authority over the armed forces. In 2019, Aung San Suu Kyi appeared at the ICJ to defend Myanmar against the allegations of genocide. Her speech in The Hague characterized the crisis as a legitimate internal conflict with a Rohingya militant group, despite an abundance of evidence that the military had targeted the whole population.

Aung San Suu Kyi was overthrown in the February 2021 military coup and jailed; she was moved into house arrest this year.

The coup sparked a civil war in which the military has been accused of further crimes against humanity throughout the country. The junta was left isolated, but more than five years later, many of Myanmar’s neighbors now seem to accept that the dictatorship—with crucial backing from China and Russia—is here to stay. President Min Aung Hlaing, who led the coup, has met with most of his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and the United States has lifted some sanctions and begun directly engaging with the regime.

A genocide verdict could complicate things, theoretically activating legal obligations for other countries to act to prevent genocide. These could include arms embargoes or sanctions that could be imposed by the United Nations Security Council, though China and Russia are likely to block any such efforts.

“An ICJ ruling does not, by itself, deliver justice,” Tom Andrews, the former U.N. special rapporteur for Myanmar, wrote in an email. “Justice requires UN member states to act, starting with the UN Security Council. If the political will existed, the Security Council would refer those responsible for the genocidal attacks against the Rohingya to the International Criminal Court. But, it doesn’t.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The bottom line is that the international community must demonstrate that a finding of genocide carries consequences. That will require that states take strong, principled action. The Rohingya deserve no less,” Andrews remarked.

According to recent reports, legal experts say the Myanmar case could also be a landmark one when it comes to the challenges of sexual violence and reparations. Sexual violence was such a trademark of the Myanmar military’s 2017 campaign that it became central to Gambia’s genocide allegation.

“The ICJ previously stated in Croatia v. Serbia that rape and other acts of sexual violence are capable of constituting genocidal acts,” Marianne Vitug, a legal advisor at the Global Justice Center who attended the Myanmar proceedings at the ICJ, wrote in an email. But in the Serbia case, the ICJ found that genocidal intent was not the “only reasonable inference” from crimes of sexual violence. (Serbia was not found directly responsible for genocide.).

“The ICJ [now] has a first-time opportunity to squarely address whether and how genocide can be committed through reproductive violence,” Vitug said.

In a recent development, gambia also made a “robust” request for reparations, Onello remarked, including domestic criminal accountability, safe return for refugees, property restoration, medical rehabilitation, recovery and reburial of bodies, protection against discrimination, and full and equal citizenship. It is the first time that a state has made a request for reparations at the ICJ on behalf of a third party; enforcement of any potential reparations would be difficult.

Finally, the case is being watched closely because of the implications that it could have for the case brought by South Africa against Israel, particularly regarding how the ICJ interprets genocidal intent.

According to recent reports, previously, intent to destroy a group needed to be the “only reasonable explanation” for the pattern of conduct to constitute genocide, Schabas noted. If a “more relaxed approach to proving genocidal intent” could be applied, then it would make a genocide verdict in the Israel case more likely, he added.

It has been revealed that vitug remarked that some members of the legal community have criticized the previous standard as unreasonably high. Gambia was “very thorough” in meeting that standard, she said, but observers are also watching to see “whether the court decides this continues to be the evidentiary standard.” The ultimate verdict will “almost certainly affect the succeeding cases,” Vitug said.

Recent findings suggest that whether U.N. commissions of inquiry are deemed permissible as evidence is another key point to watch, as they rely on a standard of “reasonable grounds to believe” that a genocide was committed rather than “beyond a reasonable doubt.” U.N. investigators determined that the Myanmar military carried out “genocidal acts” against the Rohingya. A U.N. commission of inquiry concluded that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

Those who argue against a genocide verdict in the Myanmar case point to a relatively low death toll—most estimates range between 10,000 and 25,000 out of a pre-2017 Rohingya population of 1.2 million—and say the military’s primary motivation appeared to be ejecting the Rohingya from the country rather than exterminating them.

However, Onello mentioned the extreme violence during the displacement suggests otherwise: “They surround a village. They set it on fire. They mass murder men. They mass rape women. They throw babies into the fire,” she said. “Yes, some people ran away, and they shot them in the back as they were fleeing.

Karim, who now lives in the United States, remarked she hopes that even if the ICJ doesn’t rule that Myanmar committed genocide, it acknowledges other state crimes—an unlikely outcome, since the case centers around the Genocide Convention.

Industry observers note that karim has been working with community members to manage expectations in the refugee camps in Bangladesh. “If the verdict is positive and the court decides to rule against the military, it will be a historic victory for us; however, a positive outcome doesn’t immediately repatriate the refugees or hold the military accountable,” she noted. “The piece of paper doesn’t immediately change the ground reality.”.

A verdict in the other direction—failing to hold the state responsible for genocide—wouldn’t “define the decades-long suffering we have gone through,” Karim noted.

Marco Rubio, Would-Be Pompey

  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s speech last week excoriating the rule of law, and taking particular aim at the International Criminal Court, is a sharp reminder that the United States under the Trump administration has become a rogue state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s speech last week excoriating the rule of law, and taking particular aim at the International Criminal Court, is a sharp reminder that the United States under the Trump administration has become a rogue state.

It was especially jarring to see America’s top diplomat attack the notion of international law just ahead of a three-power summit in China that will see the United States matched against—or in concert with—China and Russia. For decades, the United States has championed international law and respect for global norms as a way to contrast its behavior with rivals that carry out genocides and war crimes. That contrast is every day dimmer, by design.

Sources indicate that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s speech last week excoriating the rule of law, and taking particular aim at the International Criminal Court, is a sharp reminder that the United States under the Trump administration has become a rogue state.

It was especially jarring to see America’s top diplomat attack the notion of international law just ahead of a three-power summit in China that will see the United States matched against—or in concert with—China and Russia. For decades, the United States has championed international law and respect for global norms as a way to contrast its behavior with rivals that carry out genocides and war crimes. That contrast is every day dimmer, by design.

“At the State Department, we have seen the same thing firsthand in the realm of what is called international law. We’ve heard the concept international law invoked against nearly every major foreign-policy decision or action of this administration,” Rubio mentioned in a speech to the Federalist Society, a group of conservative lawyers. “For this global elite, international law is not a neutral body of rules; international law is an instrument, an instrument to advance their interests under the pretense of universal principles.”.

Rubio focused much of his ire on the International Criminal Court (ICC), a body created more than two decades ago to prosecute the very worst transnational crimes, including genocide and crimes against humanity. Rubio called the ICC a “fake court which is an unelected world tribunal” and cheered U.S. President Donald Trump’s sanctions on members of the court. Those sanctions, which will be fully effective in the spring, are already creating havoc for judges and prosecutors on the court.

“If they’re foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees on Americans, our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general, Pompey, when he said to those who were trying to invoke their cities’ charters against his legions. He said, ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords,’” Rubio said, a line later echoed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. (Neither man got the quote, from Plutarch, quite correct.).

The Trump administration’s cavalier approach to the rule of law is the end of an era.

Here’s what the rest of the world can do about it.

The Rohingya genocide case will have wide-ranging impacts, including for the court’s forthcoming judgment on Israel.

The jettisoning of even a modicum of respect for the rule of law was alarming to experts who have spent decades working to ensure that U.S. foreign policy upholds a rules-based system.

“I thought it was one of the most ignorant speeches given by a secretary of state I can ever recall,” said Harold Koh, who was the State Department’s legal advisor during the Obama administration and is now a professor at Yale Law School.

He noted that the opening lines of the U.S. Declaration of Independence justified the colonies’ rupture with England “out of a decent respect for the opinions of mankind.”.

“They have no appreciation for how international law has made our lives better. Nobody ever talked about air-traffic control until it broke, but international law is air-traffic control for the entire world,” Koh noted.

The actions taken by the second Trump administration had already raised concern about a rash of lawlessness in the U.S. government, as Rubio acknowledged in his speech. From the extrajudicial killings of alleged drug smugglers in the Caribbean, to the apparent targeting of civilian infrastructure in Iran, to the threats to annex Canada and Greenland, the Trump administration has long forsaken any pretense of legitimate behavior and support for international law, even when that would advance U.S. interests. Washington’s efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, for instance, and prevent Iran from regulating traffic in the waterway depend on adherence to international maritime law (as Rubio has previously noted).

Rubio’s attacks on the ICC, which codified between 1998 and 2002 the architecture of international justice that was created and carried out by the United States in the aftermath of World War II, is particularly striking. The court was created specifically to prosecute the very worst crimes, limited to genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and crimes of aggression.

In a recent development, the ICC, long a target of suspicion for U.S. conservatives who fear that a supranational body will usurp U.S. sovereignty (even though the United States is not a party to the convention or the court), has issued controversial arrest warrants for many world leaders, including two who are favorites of the Trump administration.

The ICC issued a warrant for the arrest of Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2023 for the alleged mass kidnapping of Ukrainian children during the Russia-Ukraine war and for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2024 for alleged war crimes related to the war in Gaza.

According to recent reports, ambassadors of the more than 120 countries that are parties to the Rome Statute that created the ICC met at The Hague on Wednesday to discuss how to deal with threats from the United States, among other countries. There are also fears that Washington will sanction additional international bodies, including the International Court of Justice, which is slated to rule on alleged genocide committed by the junta in Myanmar. Legal experts say that such a ruling could lower the legal threshold for genocide, which could put countries including Israel in the crosshairs of future judicial actions.

Rubio’s speech, which follows similar bellicose messages and policies from other officials such as Hegseth and U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz, show the Trump administration’s disdain for the rules that underpinned the American century, Koh said.

“International law sets default patterns of behavior. It’s like driving on the wrong side of the road—that leads to car crashes, and this leads to conflicts with allies,” Koh said.

Industry observers note that “How does attacking these institutions help us? Everybody knows the ICC is going to survive Marco Rubio,” he added.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The One Substantial Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects. The ITC is a historic renewable energy subsidy that provides a 30% tax credit against the total cost of an eligible project, and it is presently available to the commercial and utility-scale solar segments.

Recent findings suggest that A residential solar project in New York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions. Credit: Nickels Energy Solutions.

According to recent reports, after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned. However, a loophole in the tax credit language has allowed leased or “third party-owned” (TPO) solar projects to still receive the ITC (25D) on residential solar projects. In this scenario, it matters who owns the solar project, not necessarily where it’s built. The project can be subsidized because it is owned by a commercial tech giant, and not the homeowner.

Some residential solar installers are still strictly pursuing and installing privately-owned solar projects. Nickels Energy Solutions (NES), a residential solar contractor working in Central Latest York believes a privately-owned PV system is still the better deal for the customer.

Recent findings suggest that “We don’t have the same offers as some of the bigger companies,” mentioned Kevin Nickels, VP of sales with NES. “If you can offer leases, it’s like the ‘haves and have-nots.’ I don’t have that loophole or that trick up my sleeve, so it forces me to get the project sold, while I’m as sharp as I can be with margins to make it somewhat competitive.”.

TPO solar transactions are typically arranged at a lower up-front cost than a wholly owned solar project. Lease contract lengths vary by provider, and financiers have surety in these transactions because the projects will be built with products from an approved vendor list (AVL). Products on an AVL can qualify for a domestic content subsidy, another tax credit in addition to the ITC, because they are manufactured using a certain percentage of domestic components.

These are premium products vetted for AVLs. But it can also mean that installers are paying premium prices for components in building TPO solar projects.

Nickels believes that, while a privately owned residential solar project will cost more at the start, the combination of expensive components and interest rates for financing over a lease term — with factors like rate increases — can cost a customer more in the long run.

“I don’t think all leases are bad,” he said. “I just don’t think it’s what’s best for the industry or the homeowner.”.

Selling residential solar in 2026.

Sources indicate that rudy Wright, owner of Wright-Way Solar of Tyler, Texas, has shifted the company’s focus from building newly introduced projects to servicing existing systems. As the ITC exited the residential solar market, so did many of the lenders financing these projects. Without lending options, Wright-Way’s installation output has slowed down, and those clients who can afford solar are paying with cash or using a home equity loan to cover the cost.

Despite that, Wright said he isn’t very interested in building leased solar projects.

Industry observers note that wright-Way Solar built a solar plus storage project at a Ranch in Texas featuring arrays that are facing east, west and south. Credit: Wright-Way Solar.

“I do think it cost me some of those entry level clients, but every time I analyzed the financing end of it, I felt like I was benefitting my company and the industry more than the customer,” Wright mentioned. “I haven’t seen the angle where bringing a pre-purchase agreement or bringing a lease agreement has enough ironclad return for the customer.”.

It has been revealed that tyler is a unique market for solar because many of Wright-Way’s customers are trying to make their properties more resilient, and less reliant on the grid, by installing solar and storage, and not just seeking cost savings for their energy use. Wright has installed solar plus storage systems on Texan ranches at a scale close a small commercial project.

That promise of resilience is still enough reason for some people to commission a solar project in Texas, where the state’s independent electrical grid operator has faltered and experienced dangerous outages in recent years.

“Folks realize money in the bank doesn’t do you any good if the power goes out,” Wright noted.

Industry observers note that NES is still building a steady pipeline of residential solar projects in Fresh York. Nickels remarked that has been possible in part because many of its clients are upper-middle class; but New York also maintains an incentive program for solar projects, NY-Sun, which includes a 25% state tax credit for residential systems.

In a recent development, “The OBBBA caught a lot of states flat-footed,” Nickels remarked. “Without federal support, it puts a lot of pressure on what the state is offering.”.

It has been revealed that some states’ solar subsidy programs have stepped in where federal support has diminished since the OBBBA was passed. The North Carolina Clean Energy Technology Center maintains the Database of State Incentives for Renewables & Efficiency, which analyzes which states right now have policies and incentives supporting clean energy developments. Every state has policy enabling solar projects, but not necessarily cost incentives for individual projects.

While traditional residential solar projects have lost a significant subsidy, the reality is that energy costs have risen in response to latest grid demands from hyperscale data centers and oil scarcity from the United States’ war in Iran. Sure, a privately owned residential solar project won’t receive the ITC, but it can still stabilize energy costs without them.

“We lost a major incentive, but the rate increase is proportional,” Nickels noted.

Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May.
  • Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.
  • “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

“The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

In a recent development, at glitch is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”.

In a recent development, the letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of Upcoming York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

According to recent reports, advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly stated it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the matter.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

“Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

In a recent development, “Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most notable stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”.

According to recent reports, the House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the concern.

Industry observers note that “Across the political spectrum,” the letter mentioned, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”.

#42055. Why Israel Is Losing America

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2398 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

Why Israel Is Losing America

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress.
  • Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Important Ally.
  • American politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ANDREW P. MILLER is a Senior Fellow in National Security and International Policy at the Center for American Progress. He was Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Israeli-Palestinian Affairs in the Biden administration and Director for Egypt and Israel Military Concerns on the National Security Council in the Obama administration.

Only a Radical Course Change Can Win Back Its Most Important Ally.

American politicians have woken up to the fact that the public has soured on Israel. On November 3, as Americans headed to the polls, U.S. President Donald Trump made the surprising announcement that the United States would stop sending aid to Israel, valued at around $4 billion annually, by the end of the year. That night, Democrats, many of whom are increasingly outspoken in their criticism of Israeli actions, swept the House and Senate.

As I wrote in Foreign Affairs a year ago, the “exceptional relationship” between the United States and Israel, in which Israel is treated differently than any other U.S. ally or partner, is coming to an end. No other country receives the tremendous latitude and unconditional backing that the United States extends to Israel. In addition to directly hurting Palestinians, the United States’ support for Israel incentivizes reckless Israeli behavior and dubious strategic thinking. The consequences of the blank check are clear. Over the past three years, tens of thousands of Gazans have been killed, progress toward peace and reconstruction in the Gaza Strip has stalled, the annexation of the West Bank proceeds at an unprecedented rate, and the United States is stuck in an unpopular war in the Middle East with seemingly no end. Israel, for its part, is no safer than on October 6, 2023, and unquestionably more isolated.

Industry observers note that things are about to change. For better or worse, the United States will recalibrate its relationship with Israel over the coming years and a latest paradigm for the bilateral relationship will emerge—one in which Israel is expected to comply with U.S. and international law, the two countries refrain from interfering in each other’s domestic politics, and the United States limits its support when Israeli goals conflict with its own.

It has been revealed that this change is inevitable, and there is little that Israel and its supporters can do to stop it. But Israel can help keep the United States onside by making itself a reliable partner. As it begins what could be a drawn-out government formation process after last month’s elections, Israel can opt to change direction and plot a course that will not further alienate its closest ally.

Recent findings suggest that whoever leads the next Israeli government can begin rebuilding trust with the United States before a new U.S. president takes office, in 2029. It won’t be easy. Just as Americans have grown critical of Israel over the past three years, Israelis have shifted further to the right. Israel’s next leaders will need the courage to curb the country’s expansionist policies and resurrect the much-maligned two-state solution. But if they fail to overhaul their approach to Palestinians and the wider region, Israel risks losing its biggest champion and defender—perhaps for good.

Trump, who seems to delight in bullying U.S. allies and partners, has maintained the United States’ long-standing exceptional approach to Israel. He joined Israel in launching strikes on Iran in June 2025 and a larger war in February 2026, embarking for the first time on a truly joint military operation with the Jewish state. Like other presidents before him, Trump has provided Israel with bombs, missiles, and aircraft, largely with no strings attached. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also interfered in each other’s political systems to an unprecedented degree by endorsing candidates.

Time and again, Trump has deferred to Israel even when such support has run against American interests. The 2026 war on Iran is the most blatant example. Netanyahu persuaded Trump to give up nuclear talks with Iran and join a war that has failed in its objectives and upended energy markets. Even where the Trump administration has staked out U.S. priorities, it has largely refrained from trying to compel Israel to adhere to them. Israel, for example, has obstructed Trump’s peace plan for Gaza, which is meant to restore governance to the Palestinians, disarm Hamas, and lead to a permanent Israeli withdrawal from the territory. Israel has undermined the plan by expanding its military footprint in Gaza beyond the agreed demarcation lines and denying entry to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), an interim technocratic body that is intended to govern the territory under Trump’s plan and is currently marooned in Egypt. But the Trump administration has barely sounded a single note of disapproval, reinforcing Netanyahu’s long-standing view that he can defy the United States at little cost.

Moreover, it remains to be seen whether Trump will follow through on his pledge to cut military aid to Israel. The timing of his statement suggests it could have been an electoral stunt, and he remarked himself that the announcement would deprive the left of a talking point. One possibility is that the United States continues gifting Israel weapons to the tune of billions, just under a different guise. The National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027, which passed the House this summer and could pass the Senate before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress this coming January, contains a provision that would expand the Pentagon’s financial and material assistance to Israel.

According to recent reports, trump has made no effort to bring U.S. military assistance or transfers to Israel in line with what it provides to other countries. For decades, the United States has been reluctant to subject arms sales to Israel to U.S. regulations or condition them on Israeli behavior. All recent presidents, for example, have effectively exempted Israel from so-called Leahy laws, which prohibit U.S. assistance to foreign military units credibly implicated in human-rights violations. Despite rampant settler terrorism in the West Bank, in many cases facilitated by the Israeli military, the Trump administration has not indicated that it would declare any Israeli units ineligible to receive U.S. weapons.

Trump has also intervened in Israeli politics more than any other U.S. leader. He has hectored Israeli President Isaac Herzog to pardon Netanyahu so that the prime minister can escape the consequences of an ongoing corruption trial. Ahead of October’s election in Israel, Trump offered Netanyahu a “complete and total endorsement” in his bid for another term. Such blatant interference in Israel’s domestic politics not only undermines the rule of law and integrity of Israeli elections but also serves to normalize Netanyahu’s repeated interventions in U.S. domestic politics. True to form, the Israeli prime minister has praised Trump as “by far the greatest friend Israel has ever had or will have in the White House” just two weeks before the U.S. midterm elections, effectively endorsing Republican candidates for Congress. As in other areas of the relationship, Trump has made what is already an unhealthy dynamic worse.

Unconditional support from the United States has hurt Israel in a crucial way: it indulges the worst instincts of Israeli leaders and does nothing to dissuade them from their embrace of a near-perpetual state of war. After Hamas’s attack three years ago, Israel has bombed Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and even Qatar. Although Israel has dealt blows to its adversaries, there is no evidence that these wars have made Israel any safer. Iran and its proxies have been weakened, but in the course of fighting, Tehran has discovered the extent of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the global economy and appears even more interested in developing a nuclear weapon. In Lebanon, Hezbollah still poses a threat and is devising new ways of striking Israeli territory. Although confined to a smaller portion of Gaza, Hamas is reconstituting its capabilities and quashing any internal Palestinian challenge to its rule. And in the West Bank, runaway settler violence, the proliferation of illegal Israeli outposts, and the growing threat of terrorism or even a Palestinian uprising have pushed the territory to the breaking point.

Israel has also drifted ever closer to pariah status, isolated internationally thanks to its aggressive tactics. Even the country’s closest historical allies have imposed punitive measures that would have been unthinkable just five years ago. Canada, France, and the United Kingdom, for example, announced wide-ranging sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank in September. Such policies are no longer only the purview of traditional critics of Israel, such as Indonesia and Ireland.

Recent findings suggest that israel’s reputation within the United States has also tanked. According to Pew polling, 60 percent of Americans have an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 42 percent in 2022. So far, Trump has stopped Congress from restricting support for Israel—both through threatening vetoes and applying pressure on congressional Republicans—but he cannot hold back the tide of American public opinion indefinitely. Once it breaks, Israelis will have to face more than criticism from its closest ally and security guarantor. With Democrats soon to be in control of both the House and the Senate, Congress will likely pass bills that sanction settlement building and condition military aid on adherence to U.S. and international law.

Without changes in U.S. and Israeli policy, the two countries could see their relationship rupture as continued support for Israel becomes politically untenable in the United States. To rehabilitate itself in the eyes of Americans—and therefore ensure long-term cooperation with the United States—Israel will need to change course. It must abandon Netanyahu’s bludgeoning approach to both the Palestinians and the wider region.

Industry observers note that it is no exaggeration to say that the future of the U.S.-Israeli relationship rests on what type of government Israel forms in the next few months. Netanyahu’s exclusion from the next government represents the best hope for preserving bilateral relations with the United States. Netanyahu has proved unwilling to stay out of U.S. politics or modify draconian security policies that have run afoul of the American public. Unfortunately, most of Netanyahu’s rivals for prime minister share his hawkish position on the Palestinians and the Middle East. Were they in power, they seem likely to resist fundamental revisions to Israeli policy that could safeguard the bilateral relationship.

Sources indicate that israel’s next leaders need to journey outside their comfort zone. They will have to come to terms with newly introduced realities: that tensions between the United States and Israel are now deep-rooted and that they can’t rely on the adamantine support of the Republican party any longer. To win back Americans, the Israeli government will have to rigorously follow through on its commitments under Trump’s blueprint for Gaza, daring Hamas to follow suit. In addition to flooding Gaza with humanitarian aid, Israel should let the NCAG enter the territory to offer an alternative to Hamas’s rule and nihilistic agenda. Enabling the deployment of newly trained Palestinian security forces and the formation of the International Stabilization Force, a peacekeeping mission, would also help show that, whatever unfolds in Gaza, Israel is operating in good faith. Israeli forces should immediately return to the demarcation lines traced in Trump’s Gaza peace plan and pull back even further in concert with Hamas’s progress in fulfilling the terms of the plan until Israel has completely withdrawn from Gaza.

Industry observers note that israel must also rein in violent settlers in the West Bank and hold them accountable through the courts. The Israeli security services can identify the leaders and primary instigators behind the violence and should arrest them and bring them to justice. Given that settlers have killed and injured American citizens in these attacks, continued inaction by Israeli authorities is a recipe for more friction with the United States, especially if a Democratic government comes to power in Washington.

In a recent development, israel must also halt its creeping annexation of the West Bank. Over the past three years, the Netanyahu government has increased its military presence in the West Bank, deprived the Palestinian Authority of funds, asserted Israeli government control over larger swaths of Palestinian land, approved a slew of fresh Israeli settlements, and retroactively legalized illicit outposts. In sum, these actions aim to render a Palestinian state impossible. Although reversing these measures would not arrest the expansion of existing settlements and Israeli infrastructure throughout the West Bank, they would be received positively in the United States.

It has been revealed that israeli leaders also need to break the taboo around Palestinian statehood. Only a couple of decades ago, the idea of a Palestinian state was conceivable to most Israelis. Today, Israeli politicians, with precious few exceptions, cannot bring themselves to endorse a two-state solution. It will take time and no small degree of political resolve, but Israeli leaders must convince the public to accept the necessity and the virtues of a Palestinian state existing side by side with Israel. An Israel that can view Palestinians as neighbors entitled to the same rights would provide a very different image to the world than a messianic government bent on expelling whole populations.

According to recent reports, these steps will not satisfy all American critics of Israel. Anti-Israeli attitudes cannot be erased in a matter of months. Where anti-Israeli opinion intersects with anti-Semitism—evident in incidents such as a recent boycott of Jewish-owned restaurants in Philadelphia organized by the group Philly Bike on Your Left—the task is even more difficult and will necessitate a different set of policies that transcend Israel, including the formation of diverse domestic and international coalitions to identify and condemn anti-Semitic acts. Yet a far less belligerent Israel and one newly committed to the resolution of the unanswered question of Palestinian self-determination would start to shift U.S. public opinion back in the country’s favor.

It has been revealed that if Israel fails to change course, it will find itself less secure and more isolated internationally. Without access to international markets and capital, its economy, which has withstood the turmoil of the last several years remarkably well, will suffer and living standards will fall. Under these circumstances, Jewish Israeli citizens with second passports may elect to leave, depriving the state of its raison d’être—providing a safe and prosperous homeland for the Jewish people. Put simply, an Israel without American support will struggle to survive.

Chinese officials barred a Bloomberg reporter from a high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin after she asked a question during an earlier bilateral session.

According to recent reports, the clash over press access unfolded on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China, where the three leaders gathered for their first-ever three-way meeting to discuss nuclear arms control, trade and the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Hordern was blocked after she called out a question to Trump during his earlier one-on-one meeting with Xi: "President Trump, has Jensen Huang been disloyal to the United States?".

Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin take part in a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 19, 2026. According to recent reports, A second reporter also started to ask a question during the bilateral session but was shushed by Chinese officials. TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS.

Trump praised his friendship with Xi, who greeted Air Force One on the tarmac Wednesday with a one-armed hug and called Putin "my friend" ahead of a separate 40-minute sit-down.

Tensions over artificial intelligence, however, still hung over the meetings.
